blocks.text: Stamen, microsporangium and pollen grain

A flower is the reproductive unit of an angiosperm. Before any gametes meet, the plant must build the male and the female structures that will make them. This stage, everything up to the moment of fertilisation, is called **pre-fertilisation**. The male part of the flower is the **stamen**, which has a long slender stalk called the filament and a terminal, usually bilobed, structure called the anther. The proximal end of the filament is attached to the thalamus or the petal.

A typical anther is bilobed and each lobe has two theca, so it is **dithecous**. In a cross-section the anther looks four-sided (tetragonal) and has a **microsporangium** at each of the four corners, so there are four microsporangia, two in each lobe. As the anther matures the microsporangia become pollen sacs full of pollen grains.

The wall of a microsporangium has four layers. From the outside they are the **epidermis**, the **endothecium**, the **middle layers** and the **tapetum**. The outer three protect the anther and help it open (dehisce) to release pollen. The innermost layer, the tapetum, has dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus per cell, and it **nourishes the developing pollen grains**. In the centre lies the sporogenous tissue, whose cells will become the microspore mother cells.

What to learn from this figure: Remember the layer order from the outside in: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum. Only the innermost tapetum feeds the developing pollen; the outer layers protect the anther and help it open. The small circles in the centre are the sporogenous tissue that becomes the pollen mother cells.

The **pollen grain** represents the male gametophyte. It is usually spherical, about 25 to 50 micrometres across, and has a two-layered wall. The hard outer layer is the **exine**, made of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials known. It withstands high temperatures, strong acids and alkalis, and no enzyme that degrades it is known. This is why pollen is preserved well as fossils. The exine has apertures called **germ pores** where sporopollenin is absent. The inner wall is the **intine**, a thin continuous layer of cellulose and pectin.

Inside the wall, the cytoplasm is enclosed by a plasma membrane. When a pollen grain matures it holds two cells: the large **vegetative cell**, rich in food reserves with a large irregularly shaped nucleus, and the small **generative cell**, which floats in the vegetative cytoplasm, is spindle-shaped and has dense cytoplasm and a nucleus. In over 60 per cent of angiosperms the pollen is shed at this 2-celled stage. In the rest, the generative cell divides mitotically before shedding to form two male gametes, so pollen is shed 3-celled.

What to learn from this figure: Notice the hard outer exine (sporopollenin) with gaps called germ pores, and the thin intine beneath it. In this 2-celled pollen the large vegetative cell holds a small generative cell; the generative cell later divides to give the two male gametes.

The male gametophyte of a flowering plant: a haploid, two-walled structure formed inside the microsporangium that carries the vegetative cell and the generative cell (or two male gametes) to the stigma.

Pollen is rich in nutrients, and pollen products are sold as food supplements. Some pollen, such as that of *Parthenium* (carrot grass) that came to India as a contaminant with imported wheat, causes severe allergies and bronchial disorders. Pollen viability depends on the plant: in wheat and rice it is lost within 30 minutes of release, while in members of the Rosaceae, Leguminosae and Solanaceae it can last for months. Pollen can be stored for years in liquid nitrogen at $-196$ degrees Celsius, in pollen banks.
Pistil, megasporangium and embryo sac

The female part of the flower is the **pistil** (gynoecium). A pistil has three parts: the **stigma**, which is the landing platform for pollen, the **style**, an elongated slender part beneath the stigma, and the swollen basal **ovary**. Inside the ovary is the ovarian cavity (locule), and the placenta inside it bears one or more **ovules**. A flower may have one pistil (monocarpellary) or several (multicarpellary), which may be fused (syncarpous) or free (apocarpous).

The ovule is the **megasporangium**. It is attached to the placenta by a stalk called the **funicle**, and the point where the funicle meets the body of the ovule is the **hilum**. The main body is made of a mass of parenchyma called the **nucellus**, which is enclosed by one or two protective envelopes called **integuments**. The integuments leave a small opening at the tip, the **micropyle**. The end opposite the micropyle, where the nucellus, integuments and funicle meet, is the **chalaza**.

Within the nucellus, near the micropylar end, lies the **embryo sac**, the female gametophyte. A typical embryo sac is 7-celled and 8-nucleate. Three cells at the micropylar end form the **egg apparatus**: one egg cell and two **synergids**. The synergids have special thickenings at the micropylar tip called the **filiform apparatus**, which guides the pollen tube into the synergid. Three cells at the chalazal end are the **antipodals**. The large central cell has two **polar nuclei**. Because three cells are at the micropylar end, three at the chalazal end and one large central cell, there are 7 cells but 8 nuclei, since the central cell holds two.

What to learn from this figure: Count the embryo sac: three cells at the micropylar end (egg cell and two synergids), three antipodals at the chalazal end and one large central cell. That is 7 cells but 8 nuclei, because the central cell has two polar nuclei. The micropyle is the opening where the pollen tube enters.

The female gametophyte of an angiosperm, formed inside the nucellus of the ovule from the functional megaspore, which typically contains seven cells and eight nuclei: an egg, two synergids, three antipodals and a central cell with two polar nuclei.
Microsporogenesis and megasporogenesis: the two gametophytes

**Microsporogenesis** is the formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell (microspore mother cell, PMC) through meiosis. Each cell of the sporogenous tissue is potentially a PMC. A diploid PMC undergoes meiosis and produces a cluster of four haploid microspores, called a **microspore tetrad**. As the anther matures the microspores separate and develop into pollen grains. Each microspore then divides mitotically to give the vegetative and generative cells. So one PMC gives four pollen grains.

**Megasporogenesis** is the formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell (MMC). A single, large, diploid MMC differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus. It divides by meiosis and produces four haploid megaspores. In most flowering plants only **one megaspore is functional**, usually the one towards the chalazal end, and the other three degenerate. Only the functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte. This is called **monosporic development**, and its single nucleus undergoes three successive free-nuclear mitotic divisions to give 2, 4 and then 8 nuclei. Walls then form, and the arrangement of 3 + 3 cells with two polar nuclei in the large central cell is complete.

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: Both gametophytes begin from a diploid mother cell and are haploid after meiosis. One pollen mother cell gives four pollen grains, but one megaspore mother cell gives only one embryo sac, because three of the four megaspores degenerate. Meiosis makes the spores; mitosis then builds the gametophyte.
One PMC gives four pollen grains, while one MMC gives one embryo sac. Both gametophytes are haploid, and both mother cells are diploid and divide by meiosis.
Pollination: types, agents and examples
The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. It is the link between pre-fertilisation events and fertilisation.

By the source of pollen, pollination is of three kinds. In **autogamy**, pollen from an anther lands on the stigma of the same flower. In **geitonogamy**, pollen is moved from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower on the same plant. In **xenogamy** (cross-pollination), pollen comes from a flower of a different plant, so it brings genetically different pollen to the stigma. Only xenogamy brings genetically different pollen. Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination because it needs a pollinating agent, but genetically it is the same as autogamy, since the pollen comes from the same plant.

Some plants such as *Viola* (common pansy), *Oxalis* and *Commelina* produce two kinds of flowers. The normal, chasmogamous flowers have exposed anthers and stigma. The **cleistogamous** flowers never open, and the anthers and stigma lie close together, so autogamy is assured and seeds are set even without pollinators.

Pollinating agents are abiotic (wind and water) or biotic (animals). **Wind pollination (anemophily)** is common in grasses and needs light, non-sticky pollen, well-exposed stamens, large feathery stigmas to catch pollen, often a single ovule in each ovary, and many flowers packed in an inflorescence, as in the maize cob. **Water pollination (hydrophily)** is rare, found in about 30 genera, mostly monocots, such as *Vallisneria* and *Hydrilla*. In *Vallisneria* the female flower reaches the water surface on a long stalk, and the male flowers or pollen are released on the surface and carried passively to the female flower. In most aquatic plants such as water hyacinth and water lily, pollination is by insects or wind, not water.

**Insect pollination (entomophily)** is the most common biotic mode, with bees as the chief agents; flies, beetles, butterflies, moths, birds and bats also pollinate. Insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar, and the pollen grains are generally sticky. Small flowers become conspicuous by clustering in an inflorescence. Nectar and pollen are the floral rewards for the visiting animal.

blocks.text: Outbreeding devices
Continued self-pollination leads to inbreeding depression, so most flowering plants have evolved **outbreeding devices** that discourage autogamy and encourage cross-pollination. These are:

1. **Asynchrony**: pollen is released before the stigma becomes receptive, or the stigma becomes receptive much before pollen is released.
2. **Different positions**: the anther and stigma are placed at different heights so that pollen cannot easily fall on the stigma of the same flower.
3. **Self-incompatibility**: a genetic mechanism that prevents pollen of the same flower or plant from fertilising the ovules, because the pistil rejects it.
4. **Unisexual flowers**: if male and female flowers are on the same plant (monoecious, as in castor and maize), autogamy is prevented but geitonogamy is not. If they are on different plants (dioecious, as in papaya), both autogamy and geitonogamy are prevented.
Do not call cleistogamy an outbreeding device. It is the opposite: it guarantees self-pollination. Also remember that monoecy stops only autogamy, while dioecy stops both autogamy and geitonogamy.
Pollen-pistil interaction

Pollination does not guarantee fertilisation. The pistil can recognise whether the pollen landing on it is the right type, compatible, or the wrong type, incompatible. This dialogue of chemical signals is the **pollen-pistil interaction**. If the pollen is compatible, the pistil accepts it and promotes post-pollination events. If it is incompatible, the pistil rejects it, preventing pollen germination or pollen tube growth.

After a compatible pollen grain lands on the stigma, it germinates and the intine grows out through a germ pore as the **pollen tube**. The tube grows through the tissues of the stigma and style and reaches the ovary. The generative cell divides, if it has not already done so, to form two male gametes, which travel in the pollen tube. The pollen tube usually enters the ovule through the micropyle, a path called **porogamy**, passes through one synergid via the filiform apparatus and releases the two male gametes into the synergid.

In **artificial hybridisation**, breeders get only the desired pollen on the stigma by two steps. **Emasculation** is the removal of anthers from the bud of the female parent before they dehisce, and **bagging** covers the flower with a bag of suitable size, often butter paper, to prevent contamination from unwanted pollen. When the stigma is receptive, the desired pollen is dusted on it, and the flower is bagged again until the fruit develops.
Double fertilisation

In the synergid, the two male gametes are released. One male gamete moves towards the egg cell and fuses with it. This is **syngamy**, and it forms the diploid **zygote**. The other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell. Because three haploid nuclei are involved, this is called **triple fusion**, and it forms the triploid **primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)**. The central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell. Since two types of fusion, syngamy and triple fusion, occur in one embryo sac, the event is called **double fertilisation**. It is a unique feature of flowering plants.

What to learn from this figure: Follow the two male gametes (green) released into a synergid. One fuses with the egg (syngamy) to make the diploid zygote; the other fuses with the two polar nuclei (triple fusion) to make the triploid primary endosperm nucleus. Remember n + n = 2n for the zygote and n + n + n = 3n for the PEN.

The sequence of two fusion events in an embryo sac of a flowering plant: syngamy of one male gamete with the egg to form the zygote, and triple fusion of the second male gamete with two polar nuclei to form the primary endosperm nucleus.

blocks.problem: A plant has a diploid chromosome number of 2n = 20. State the number of chromosomes in (a) a pollen grain, (b) a synergid, (c) the zygote and (d) a cell of the endosperm.
blocks.solution: Both gametophytes are haploid, so a pollen grain and a synergid, which belong to the male and female gametophytes, have n = 10 chromosomes. The zygote forms by fusion of a haploid egg (10) and a haploid male gamete (10), so it has 10 + 10 = 20. The primary endosperm nucleus forms by triple fusion of two polar nuclei (10 each) with one male gamete (10), so it has 10 + 10 + 10 = 30 chromosomes, and every endosperm cell that arises from it by mitosis also has 30.

blocks.text: Post-fertilisation: development of endosperm and embryo

After double fertilisation, events in the ovule and ovary begin: development of endosperm and embryo, maturation of ovule into seed and of ovary into fruit. **Endosperm develops before the embryo**, because it provides the nutrition for the growing embryo. The PEN divides repeatedly. In the most common type, **free-nuclear endosperm**, the nuclei divide without wall formation, so many free nuclei lie in the cytoplasm. Later, cell walls form and the endosperm becomes **cellular**. The tender coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm, and the surrounding white kernel is cellular endosperm.

The zygote usually divides only after some endosperm has formed. It passes through the **proembryo** stage and the globular and heart-shaped stages to the mature embryo. A typical **dicot embryo** has an embryonal axis and two cotyledons. The part of the axis above the cotyledons is the **epicotyl**, which ends in the plumule (future shoot tip). The part below is the **hypocotyl**, which ends in the radicle covered by a root cap. In grasses (monocots) the embryo has **one cotyledon**, the **scutellum**, situated towards one side of the axis. The radicle and root cap are enclosed in a sheath called the **coleorhiza**, and the plumule is enclosed in a **coleoptile**.
Formation of seed and fruit; parthenocarpy

The ovule matures into the **seed**, and the ovary develops into the **fruit**. The integuments harden to form the protective seed coats, the outer **testa** and the inner **tegmen**. The micropyle stays as a small pore that helps water and oxygen enter during germination. The ovary wall becomes the pericarp of the fruit. In most seeds the endosperm is consumed by the developing embryo, so such seeds are **non-endospermic**, as in pea, bean and groundnut. In **endospermic** seeds the endosperm persists, as in castor, wheat, maize and coconut. Occasionally a part of the nucellus persists as **perisperm**, as in black pepper and beet.

In most plants only the ovary becomes the fruit; this is a **true fruit**. In some, such as apple, strawberry and cashew, the thalamus also contributes to the fruit, so it is a **false fruit**. Fruits generally develop only after fertilisation. **Parthenocarpy** is the development of fruit without fertilisation, giving seedless fruits, as in banana. Parthenocarpy can be induced by the application of growth hormones such as auxins, as in seedless grapes.
Significance of seed in angiosperms

Seeds are the final product of sexual reproduction in a flowering plant and bring many advantages. Pollination and fertilisation do not depend on water, unlike in lower plants, so seeds give reliable reproduction. They have **better adaptive strategies for dispersal** to new habitats and help the species to colonise new areas. They hold food reserves in the endosperm or cotyledons, so the young seedling is nourished until it can photosynthesise. The hard seed coat protects the young embryo. Seeds are the product of sexual fusion and therefore carry **new genetic combinations**, which give variations. Seeds are the means by which we store the species: because they dehydrate and the embryo becomes dormant, they can be stored for years and used when required, and they provide food for humans throughout the year.

Some seeds remain viable for extremely long periods. A seed of the arctic lupin (*Lupinus arcticus*) from the Arctic tundra germinated after about 10,000 years of dormancy, and a date palm (*Phoenix dactylifera*) seed about 2,000 years old, found in an archaeological dig at Herod's palace near the Dead Sea, germinated.
Apomixis and polyembryony
A form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction: seeds are produced without fertilisation. It is seen in some species of Asteraceae and grasses.

Apomixis may occur in more than one way. In some species the diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation. In many *Citrus* and mango varieties, some nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing and protrude into the embryo sac to form embryos, which is **adventive embryony**. Such a seed has more than one embryo, a condition called **polyembryony**. When the seedlings from such a seed are raised, the nucellar embryo is genetically identical to the parent, as it comes from diploid somatic nucellar cells.

Apomixis is important in hybrid seed production. Hybrids show hybrid vigour, but their seeds segregate in the next generation, so farmers must buy fresh hybrid seeds each year, which is costly. If a hybrid is made apomictic, there is no segregation of characters in the progeny, and the farmer can keep using the seeds of the hybrid year after year, which reduces the cost of seed. Scientists are trying to transfer apomixis genes to commercial hybrids.

blocks.problem: A single anther of a plant has 150 pollen mother cells and each pollen grain is shed at the 3-celled stage. How many pollen grains and how many male gametes are formed from this anther?
blocks.solution: Each pollen mother cell is diploid and divides by meiosis to form four haploid microspores, and each microspore becomes one pollen grain. So the number of pollen grains is 150 x 4 = 600. A 3-celled pollen grain contains one vegetative cell and two male gametes, since the generative cell has already divided. Therefore the number of male gametes is 600 x 2 = 1200.

blocks.text: Common mistakes: (1) writing that the embryo sac has 8 cells (it has 7 cells and 8 nuclei); (2) forgetting that the endosperm is triploid; (3) saying geitonogamy is genetically cross-pollination, when it is genetically autogamy; (4) calling the tapetum the outermost layer of the anther wall, when it is the innermost; (5) confusing parthenocarpy (fruit without fertilisation) with apomixis (seed without fertilisation).

diagrams.caption: Microsporangium wall layers (schematic)
diagrams.description: Schematic transverse section of one microsporangium. From the outside inward the layers are the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum. The centre is the sporogenous tissue, drawn as small circles, whose cells become pollen mother cells. The tapetum is the layer that nourishes the developing pollen grains.

diagrams.alt: Pollen grain with a thick exine, a thin intine, two germ pores, a large vegetative cell and a small generative cell
diagrams.caption: Structure of a 2-celled pollen grain (schematic)
diagrams.description: Schematic round pollen grain. The outer wall, the exine, is thick and made of sporopollenin, with gaps called germ pores. Inside it lies the thin intine of cellulose and pectin. The cytoplasm holds a large vegetative cell with a large nucleus and a small spindle-shaped generative cell.

diagrams.alt: Ovule showing micropyle, integuments, nucellus, chalaza, funicle and the 7-celled embryo sac
diagrams.caption: Ovule and the 7-celled, 8-nucleate embryo sac (schematic)
diagrams.description: Schematic ovule. Two integuments enclose the nucellus and leave the micropyle at the top; the chalaza is at the opposite end and the funicle joins the ovule to the placenta. Inside the nucellus the embryo sac has two synergids and the egg cell at the micropylar end, a large central cell with two polar nuclei, and three antipodal cells at the chalazal end.

diagrams.alt: Flow chart comparing development of the male gametophyte from a pollen mother cell and the female gametophyte from a megaspore mother cell
diagrams.caption: Male and female gametophyte development
diagrams.description: Two columns. Male: a diploid pollen mother cell divides by meiosis into a tetrad of four haploid microspores; each microspore divides by mitosis to become a pollen grain with a vegetative and a generative cell. Female: a diploid megaspore mother cell divides by meiosis into four haploid megaspores, of which one is functional; its nucleus divides by three mitoses to give 8 nuclei and the 7-celled embryo sac.

diagrams.alt: Pollen tube releasing two male gametes into a synergid; one fuses with the egg and one with the two polar nuclei
diagrams.caption: Double fertilisation in the embryo sac (schematic)
diagrams.description: Schematic embryo sac with a pollen tube entering one synergid. The two male gametes released there move in different directions: one fuses with the egg cell by syngamy to form the diploid zygote, and the other fuses with the two polar nuclei in the central cell by triple fusion to form the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.

questions.stem: A typical angiosperm anther, which is bilobed and dithecous, has how many microsporangia?
questions.explanation: A typical anther is bilobed and each lobe has two theca, so the anther is dithecous. In cross-section it is tetragonal, with one microsporangium at each corner, giving four microsporangia in all, two in each lobe, which later become pollen sacs.

optionRationale.1: Two is the number of microsporangia in each lobe, not in the whole anther.
optionRationale.3: No standard anther has six microsporangia.
optionRationale.4: Eight is not a number found in a normal anther.

questions.objective: State the number of microsporangia in a typical anther

questions.stem: Which layer of the wall of a microsporangium nourishes the developing pollen grains?
questions.explanation: The wall of a microsporangium has epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and tapetum from outside inwards. The tapetum is the innermost layer and has dense cytoplasm, and it nourishes the developing pollen grains. The outer layers protect the anther and help it to open.

optionRationale.1: The epidermis is the outermost protective layer and has no nutritive role.
optionRationale.2: The endothecium lies below the epidermis and helps in the dehiscence of the anther.
optionRationale.4: This lies inside the wall, and its cells become microspore mother cells; it is not a wall layer.

questions.objective: Identify the function of the tapetum

questions.stem: The typical mature embryo sac of a flowering plant has
questions.explanation: The embryo sac has three cells at the micropylar end (the egg and two synergids), three antipodal cells at the chalazal end and one large central cell. That makes seven cells. The central cell holds two polar nuclei, so the total number of nuclei is eight.

optionRationale.2: The numbers are reversed; the sac has more nuclei than cells.
optionRationale.3: The central cell has two polar nuclei, so the nuclei number one more than the cells.
optionRationale.4: There are only seven cells, because the two polar nuclei lie together in one central cell.

questions.objective: State the structure of the mature embryo sac

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Pollen grains are well preserved as fossils.
Reason (R): The exine of a pollen grain is made of sporopollenin, which resists high temperature, strong acids and alkalis and enzymatic degradation.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Sporopollenin in the exine is an extremely resistant organic material that no known enzyme degrades, so pollen survives for a very long time in sediments. Both statements are true, and the resistance of the exine directly explains why pollen is found as fossils.

optionRationale.2: R is not just true but also the direct reason for the fossil record of pollen.
optionRationale.3: R is true; sporopollenin really is highly resistant.
optionRationale.4: A is true; pollen fossils are well known.

questions.objective: Relate the exine's sporopollenin to the fossil record of pollen

questions.stem: In maize the diploid chromosome number is 20. How many chromosomes are present in a cell of its endosperm?
questions.explanation: The endosperm arises from the primary endosperm nucleus, formed by triple fusion of two haploid polar nuclei and one haploid male gamete. With n = 10, the number is 10 + 10 + 10 = 30, which is 3n. The endosperm is therefore triploid.

optionRationale.1: Ten is the haploid number, found in the egg or male gamete, not in the endosperm.
optionRationale.2: Twenty is the diploid number of the zygote and of the body cells.
optionRationale.3: Forty would be a tetraploid cell; endosperm is triploid, not tetraploid.

questions.objective: Compute the chromosome number of endosperm

questions.stem: Transfer of pollen from the anther of one flower to the stigma of another flower of the same plant is called geitonogamy. It is
options: genetically similar to autogamy but ecologically cross-pollination
questions.explanation: In geitonogamy the pollen comes from the same plant, so genetically it is the same as autogamy and there is no new variation. But the pollen moves between two different flowers and needs a pollinating agent, so it functions as cross-pollination.

optionRationale.1: This reverses the facts: the pollen comes from the same plant, so it is genetically self.
optionRationale.2: The pollen is not genetically different from the plant's own stigma.
optionRationale.4: Geitonogamy needs an agent such as an insect or the wind to carry the pollen between flowers, so it is not functionally autogamy.

questions.objective: Distinguish geitonogamy from autogamy and xenogamy

questions.stem: Match List-I (mode of pollination) with List-II (feature or example) and choose the correct code.

right: II. Sticky pollen and fragrant, nectar-rich flowers
III. Flowers that never open, as in Viola and Commelina
IV. Light non-sticky pollen and large feathery stigma

questions.explanation: Wind-pollinated flowers have light, non-sticky pollen and feathery stigmas (A-IV). Water pollination occurs in Vallisneria (B-I). Insect-pollinated flowers have sticky pollen and attract insects with nectar and fragrance (C-II). Cleistogamous flowers, as in Viola and Commelina, never open (D-III).

optionRationale.1: A and B are interchanged: Vallisneria is water pollinated, not wind pollinated.
optionRationale.3: B and C are interchanged: sticky pollen belongs to insect pollination and Vallisneria to water.

questions.objective: Match pollination modes with their characteristic features

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about double fertilisation in a flowering plant.
A. Syngamy forms a diploid zygote.
B. Triple fusion forms a triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
C. Both male gametes fuse with the egg cell.
D. The antipodal cells fuse with the second male gamete.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: One male gamete fuses with the haploid egg and gives the diploid zygote (A). The second male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei of the central cell, giving the triploid primary endosperm nucleus (B). Only one gamete enters the egg, and the antipodals take no part in fertilisation.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is wrong: only one male gamete fuses with the egg.
optionRationale.2: Statement D is wrong: the second male gamete fuses with the polar nuclei, not the antipodals.
optionRationale.3: C is wrong, so this combination fails.

questions.objective: Analyse the events of double fertilisation

questions.stem: The functional megaspore of an angiosperm develops into the 8-nucleate embryo sac by how many successive mitotic divisions of its nucleus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides mitotically to give 2 nuclei, then 4, then 8. These are three successive divisions, since 2 to the power 3 is 8. The nuclei then organise into seven cells, with the two polar nuclei in the central cell.

optionRationale.1: Two divisions give only four nuclei.
optionRationale.2: Four divisions would give sixteen nuclei.
optionRationale.4: One division gives only two nuclei.

questions.objective: Count the mitotic divisions in embryo sac formation

questions.stem: A plant has 2n = 16. The number of chromosomes in the functional megaspore, in an antipodal cell and in a cell of the endosperm are respectively
questions.explanation: The functional megaspore is a product of meiosis, so it is haploid, n = 8. Antipodals arise from it by mitosis and are also haploid, n = 8. The endosperm forms by triple fusion of two polar nuclei (8 each) and one male gamete (8), giving 3n = 24.

optionRationale.1: The functional megaspore is haploid, so 16 is wrong for it.
optionRationale.3: An antipodal cell is part of the haploid gametophyte, so it has 8, not 16.

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Tender coconut water is the free-nuclear endosperm of the coconut.
Reason (R): In free-nuclear endosperm, repeated divisions of the primary endosperm nucleus are not followed by cell wall formation, so many free nuclei lie in the liquid cytoplasm.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: In the common type of endosperm development, the triploid PEN divides repeatedly without wall formation, and the free nuclei lie in a liquid. Later the endosperm becomes cellular and forms the white kernel. R describes exactly why the endosperm is liquid, so it explains A.

optionRationale.2: R is not merely related; it is the direct explanation for the liquid nature of the endosperm.
optionRationale.3: R is correct; wall formation is delayed in free-nuclear endosperm.
optionRationale.4: A is correct; coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm.

questions.objective: Explain why coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm

questions.stem: An anther has 240 pollen mother cells, and all pollen grains are shed at the 3-celled stage. Assuming every cell completes its development, how many male gametes are produced in the anther?
questions.explanation: Each pollen mother cell gives four microspores by meiosis, so 240 x 4 = 960 pollen grains. Each 3-celled pollen grain contains two male gametes, since the generative cell has divided. So the total is 960 x 2 = 1920 male gametes.

optionRationale.1: This is the number of pollen grains (240 x 4), not male gametes; each 3-celled grain holds two gametes.
optionRationale.2: This counts only two products per mother cell.
optionRationale.3: This is the number of pollen mother cells, not male gametes.

questions.objective: Compute male gametes from pollen mother cells

questions.stem:
Which of the following statements about outbreeding devices are correct?
A. Dioecy prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
B. Monoecy prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy.
C. Self-incompatibility is a genetic mechanism that stops self-pollen from fertilising ovules of the same plant.
D. Cleistogamy promotes cross-pollination.
questions.explanation: In dioecious plants like papaya the male and female flowers are on separate plants, so both autogamy and geitonogamy are blocked. In monoecious plants like castor, pollen can move between flowers of the same plant, so only autogamy is blocked. Self-incompatibility is a genetic block. Cleistogamy ensures self-pollination, so D is false.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is also correct, so this misses it.
optionRationale.3: A is correct but excluded here, and D is false.
optionRationale.4: B is correct but excluded here, and D is false.

questions.stem: A plant breeder wants a hybrid crop whose seeds can be saved and sown every year without losing the hybrid characters. Which process should be introduced into the hybrid?
questions.explanation: Apomixis produces seeds without meiosis or fertilisation, so the progeny are genetically identical to the hybrid parent and do not segregate. Farmers can then use hybrid seeds from their own crop each year, reducing seed cost. Parthenocarpy yields seedless fruits, and pollination types give segregating progeny.

optionRationale.1: Parthenocarpy gives seedless fruit, so there are no seeds to save.
optionRationale.2: Cleistogamy causes self-pollination, which leads to segregation and loss of hybrid vigour.
optionRationale.4: Geitonogamy is pollination within a plant, which leads to segregation in the progeny.

questions.objective: Apply apomixis to hybrid seed production

questions.stem: In black pepper and beet, a persistent remnant of the nucellus is found in the seed. It is called
questions.explanation: In most seeds the nucellus is used up during development. In some, such as black pepper and beet, a part of it remains as a persistent tissue called perisperm. It is of maternal origin, and it should not be confused with endosperm, which is formed after double fertilisation.

optionRationale.2: Endosperm is formed after fertilisation from the primary endosperm nucleus, not from the nucellus.
optionRationale.3: The tegmen is the inner seed coat that develops from the integument.
optionRationale.4: The coleorhiza is the sheath around the radicle in a monocot embryo.
